planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath a high conifer canopy; Pacific dogwood resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so choose a permanent site for young nursery stock rather than planning to move it later.

directions: Pacific dogwood is the West Coast counterpart to the familiar eastern flowering dogwood, growing as a large native understory tree beneath towering Douglas-fir and western hemlock canopies from British Columbia south through California's coastal ranges and Sierra foothills. Its showy spring bracts are the largest of any North American dogwood, typically four to seven per flower cluster rather than the four found on Cornus florida, and established trees often produce a lighter second flush of bloom in late summer. The species is notably more susceptible to dogwood anthracnose than its eastern relative, so give it good air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation, and site it in filtered light rather than deep, still shade. Knobby clusters of orange-red fruit ripen in fall and are quickly taken by band-tailed pigeons, varied thrushes, and other native birds.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Cornus nuttallii
USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System — Cornus nuttallii

common_name: Eddie's White Wonder Dogwood (Hybrid Pacific x Flowering Dogwood)
scientific_name: Cornus nuttallii x florida 'Eddie's White Wonder'

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath taller trees; Eddie's White Wonder shows better resistance to dogwood anthracnose than straight Pacific dogwood but still benefits from good air circulation and a site sheltered from harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Eddie's White Wonder is a hybrid dogwood raised by Vancouver, British Columbia nurseryman Henry M. Eddie from a cross between native Pacific dogwood and the eastern flowering dogwood, combining the outsized bracts of the West Coast species with the reliable single spring flush and easier culture of Cornus florida. In mid-spring the bare branches are covered in creamy white, four- to six-bracted flowers larger than typical flowering dogwood blooms, followed by handsome dark green summer foliage that turns rich red-purple in autumn. It grows as a clean, upright, oval small tree with attractive patchy, exfoliating bark that adds winter interest, and it tolerates the dappled light of a woodland understory better than most flowering dogwoods. Avoid wounding the trunk when mowing or staking nearby, since dogwood borers readily enter through bark injuries.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Flowering Dogwood and Hybrids
University of British Columbia Botanical Garden — Cornus introductions

common_name: Colrigo Giant Pacific Dogwood (Large-Bracted Pacific Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath a high canopy; Colrigo Giant transplants poorly once established like the species, so choose a permanent site for young stock and avoid disturbing the roots later.

directions: Colrigo Giant is a selection of Pacific dogwood chosen for producing some of the largest flower bracts in the species, often six inches or more across, giving an even more dramatic spring display than typical wild seedlings of this already showy West Coast native. Like the species, it grows naturally as an understory or canopy-edge tree beneath taller conifers from British Columbia to California, and it flowers most heavily with filtered or morning sun rather than continuous deep shade. It shares the species' vulnerability to dogwood anthracnose, so provide good air circulation, keep foliage dry by avoiding overhead irrigation, and site it in well-drained soil. Because Pacific dogwood resents root disturbance, plant young container-grown stock in its permanent location rather than planning to move it later.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Cornus nuttallii
Great Plant Picks — Cornus nuttallii selections

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to deep shade beneath a conifer or mixed-forest canopy; Pacific yew is extremely slow growing and best purchased as nursery stock rather than grown from seed, since seed requires a lengthy warm-then-cold stratification and may take two years or more to germinate.

directions: Pacific yew is one of the most shade-tolerant conifers in North America, persisting for centuries as a slow-growing understory tree beneath old-growth Douglas-fir and western hemlock from southeast Alaska down through the Pacific Northwest and into the Sierra Nevada and northern Rockies. It gained sudden fame in the late twentieth century as the original source of paclitaxel (Taxol), a chemotherapy compound extracted from its bark, which triggered heavy wild harvest until semi-synthetic production methods relieved pressure on natural populations. The tree is dioecious, with female plants producing small, bright red, fleshy arils around each seed in fall that are eaten by grouse and thrushes, but as with other yews the seed itself and all other plant parts are toxic to humans and livestock if ingested, so keep foliage and clippings away from grazing animals. Its fine, dark, flattened needles and reddish-purple, peeling bark make it a handsome, if very slow-growing, specimen for the deepest shade of a naturalistic woodland garden.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System — Taxus brevifolia
Oregon State University Extension — Pacific Yew
National Cancer Institute — Paclitaxel (Taxol) Development History

common_name: Pacific Fire Vine Maple (Red-Barked Vine Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or small trees in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pacific Fire colors most vividly on bare winter wood when it gets a few hours of direct winter sun, while summer part shade keeps the foliage from scorching.

directions: Pacific Fire is a stem-color selection of vine maple, the native understory maple of Pacific Northwest conifer forests, chosen by an Oregon nursery for bright coral-red bark that glows on bare winter branches much like a red-twig dogwood. Give it at least a few hours of direct winter sun for the most vivid stem color, since plants grown in continuous deep shade tend toward a duller orange-brown, while part shade during the growing season keeps the foliage from scorching and mimics the dappled light of its native forest-edge habitat. Like the species, it has a graceful, layered, multi-stemmed habit and rounded, seven- to nine-lobed leaves that turn gold, orange, and scarlet in fall before dropping to reveal the colorful winter framework. It combines well with evergreen conifers and ferns in a Pacific Northwest-style woodland garden, where the winter bark provides color long after deciduous companions have gone dormant.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Vine Maple

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or small trees in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath taller conifers or deciduous trees; Monroe's finely cut foliage scorches more readily than the species in hot sun or drought, so a shaded, sheltered site is best.

directions: Monroe is a fernleaf selection of vine maple, its rounded leaves cut nearly to the midrib into narrow, deeply toothed lobes that give the whole canopy a lacy, refined texture quite different from the broader, more typically maple-shaped leaves of the wild species. It grows with the same graceful, arching, multi-stemmed habit as species vine maple, forming an understory large shrub or small tree well suited to the dappled shade beneath conifers or taller deciduous trees, and the finely cut foliage turns shades of gold and red in autumn. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, since vine maple's shallow, fibrous roots quickly show stress in drought or compacted ground. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing stems, since the layered, naturally sculptural branching is part of its appeal.
